text:
The Kansas City Chiefs‘ preseason if officially over and now the attention turns to Week 1. First, the Chiefs will need to finalize the team’s roster ahead of the NFL deadline on Sunday, August 30.

Additionally, the Chiefs continue to deal with injury concerns for one of the team’s key players. Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons is dealing with a back injury.

Head coach Andy Reid was vague about Simmons’ potential return timeline but indicated that the tackle remains in pain. Reid noted that Simmons’ injury could “take a little bit of time” to heal.

It is less than ideal news with the NFL season nearly two weeks away from starting.

“It’s going to take a little bit of time here, but he’s a hard worker when it comes to these type of things,” Reid told reporters on August 28.

“… It’s just a matter of eliminating some of the pain that he has and (assessing his) strength. Making sure he has enough strength there.”

Chiefs News: Kansas City Is Assessing Whether LT Josh Simmons Is Dealing With a Long-Term Injury

The news comes as Patrick Mahomes is set to return from a season-ending ACL injury. Protecting Mahomes is of high importance, and Simmons is expected to be responsible for the quarterback’s blindside.

Now, Simmons’ status for Week 1 could be in doubt if the left tackle is not able to recover soon. ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported that the Chiefs are assessing whether Simmons is dealing with a long-term injury.

“Josh Simmons, this one is interesting because he’s got a back issue,” Fowler explained on an August 27, edition of “SportsCenter.” “He’s been classified as day to day, but I can say that he is undergoing more tests to see if there is something long term here. So this could be one to watch.

“They have Jaylon Moore who’s kind of like their swing, right tackle, left tackle. He could start there if needed. So, (the injury) could be minor, but they’re still identifying that situation,” Fowler continued.

“That would be big. They’re a much better offense when he’s in there.”

The Chiefs Face Offensive Line Questions Amid Patrick Mahomes’ Return

Kansas City has high hopes for Simmons after selecting the offensive lineman in the first round of the 2025 NFL draft. Yet, Simmons played just eight games during his rookie season in 2025.

It would be less than ideal for Simmons to miss time to start the season. This is especially true with Mahomes returning from a serious injury.

Mahomes previously stated that Simmons has a chance to be one of the NFL’s top left tackles.

“He’s a ‘dawg’ at the end of the day,” Mahomes noted on an August 2025, interview on “Up and Adams,” via On3. “I mean, he’s obviously working through being an NFL pro and being a veteran, but when it comes to just pass blocking and run blocking, he can get the job done.

“… I think it’s just you hear the defensive guys talk about him, and they all are saying the right things when you want a guy that’s going to go out there and contribute,” Mahomes added.

“And so, the sky’s the limit. He has a chance to be one of the best there is at that left tackle position, but he’s got to go out there and prove that in the regular season.”

title: Commanders final 53-man roster projection: Tough choice at WR, help needed on O-line
description:
The Commanders’ revamped roster showed promise early in training camp, especially on defense, where the team made its biggest offseason investments.
That also made the team’s initial 53-man roster, due by 6 p.m. Sunday, vulnerable to significant change before that first game.
My initial roster projection for Washington is just that — an early iteration but not the final roster for Week 1.
(Note: NFL teams can designate for return up to two players who are placed on injured reserve on roster cutdown day.
Those count toward teams’ maximum of eight IR players designated for return, but do not count against the team’s roster cap.
text:
In the 237 days since last season ended, the Commanders have overhauled their systems, replaced their play callers, and changed some of their coaching staff and much of their roster in hopes of rediscovering a winning formula.

The team that made it to the NFC Championship Game two years ago is once again in rebuild mode — but with higher stakes. Coach Dan Quinn’s future in Washington may depend on a winning season, and the window to build around quarterback Jayden Daniels while he’s on his rookie contract will soon close.

The Commanders’ revamped roster showed promise early in training camp, especially on defense, where the team made its biggest offseason investments. But a slew of injuries to starters and some key reserves limited their on-field work together and created uncertainty about who will be available when the season opens Sept. 13 in Philadelphia.

That also made the team’s initial 53-man roster, due by 6 p.m. Sunday, vulnerable to significant change before that first game. Washington is seventh in the NFL’s waiver list priority order, which means it’ll have a fairly early crack at claiming, say, an interior offensive lineman (or two) or landing other quality players waived by other teams.

My initial roster projection for Washington is just that — an early iteration but not the final roster for Week 1.

(Note: NFL teams can designate for return up to two players who are placed on injured reserve on roster cutdown day. Those count toward teams’ maximum of eight IR players designated for return, but do not count against the team’s roster cap. They are eligible to return after four games. Anyone else placed on injured reserve before the 6 p.m. deadline on Sunday is done for the season.)

Offense (26)

Quarterback (3): Jayden Daniels, Marcus Mariota, Athan Kaliakmanis

Hey, shocker, Daniels is still the starter! In all seriousness, Daniels had an exceptional camp. He’s shown more and more every offseason, but this one was especially notable because of the new scheme and all that he was asked to change or do more of in offensive coordinator David Blough’s system. His transition to playing more under center appeared seamless, and his command of the offense was what you’d expect from a veteran with multiple years in a scheme.

Mariota returned on a one-year deal, ensuring continuity in the quarterback room amid all the other offensive changes.

The notable name here, though, is Kaliakmanis, a seventh-round rookie from Rutgers whose play in the first two preseason games earned him a spot here. Washington kept three quarterbacks on its initial roster the last two seasons, and with Mariota recovering from an MCL sprain, doing so again may be wise. Quinn has said he’s optimistic the veteran will be available for Week 1, but it’s not yet a certainty.

Whether Kaliakmanis sticks at the No. 3 for the season may depend on who comes available after roster cuts.

Running back (3): Jacory “Bill” Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White, Kaytron Allen

Washington released veteran Jerome Ford with an injury settlement and Jeremy McNichols suffered a “pretty good quad injury” in camp, according to Quinn. I didn’t include him on the belief he would clear waivers and be available to re-sign to the practice squad.

Allen had an up-and-down preseason — he had 85 rushing yards and a touchdown against Miami but fumbled on Washington’s opening snap in Baltimore — but his potential and draft status (sixth-round pick) ensure he stays. Undrafted rookie Robert Henry impressed in the opener against Miami, but he may not have shown enough to put Washington at risk of losing him on waivers.

Wide receiver (7): Terry McLaurin, Stefon Diggs, Antonio Williams, Treylon Burks, Dyami Brown, Jaylin Lane, Luke McCaffrey

Receiver was one of Washington’s most questionable positions before training camp, but the arrival of Diggs turned it into one of the most competitive.

McLaurin, Diggs and third-round rookie Williams were locks for the roster, leaving eight wideouts vying for three or four spots. Brown got the nod because of his speed and rapport with Daniels. Burks’ big-play ability won him a spot, and Lane made it because of his punt returns. I admittedly waffled about keeping McCaffrey. He had a very good camp and doubles as the team’s leading kick returner, but I wondered if he showed enough to hold his spot. I kept him because of his draft status (third round in 2024), his consistency compared to others and the value he provides over, say, a fifth linebacker or 10th offensive lineman.

Tight end (4): Chig Okonkwo, John Bates, Ben Sinnott, Colson Yankoff

It was always going to be these four. Yankoff had a good camp, showing his pass-catching ability on offense while remaining a special teams staple, and the others were locks before camp opened.

Offensive line (9): LT Brandon Coleman, LG Chris Paul, C Nick Allegretti, RG Sam Cosmi, RT Josh Conerly Jr., OT Andrew Wylie, OL Trent Scott, D.J. Humphries, C Matt Gulbin

*Laremy Tunsil placed on injured reserve with a designation to return

This is the group that figures to change before the opener. It needs to change. Washington cut center Tyler Biadasz in February and didn’t sign another veteran in the offseason, essentially leaving the job to Allegretti, a versatile vet who has played primarily guard. But a calf injury sidelined Allegretti for almost all of camp and his status for the opener is still not clear. Also unclear: His ability as a full-time starter at center.

Julian Good-Jones and Gulbin, a sixth-round rookie, struggled mightily in place of Allegretti, hindering the run game and leaving Daniels exposed for much of the Commanders’ joint practice with the Ravens.

Gulbin stays on the roster largely because the team invested a draft pick in him, but it wasn’t a high enough one to keep him here long-term. Washington should add another center and more help at guard since Coleman shifted back outside to left tackle after Tunsil’s injury.

Tunsil is an obvious candidate for IR with a designation for return on cutdown day. He underwent surgery to repair a torn triceps on Aug. 8, but the team left open the possibility of him returning this season. That injury typically has a 3 to 4-month recovery, depending on the severity and type of repair.

Defense (24)

Defensive line (6): Daron Payne, Javon Kinlaw, Tim Settle, Charles Omenihu, Shy Tuttle, Byron Cowart

*Johnny Newton is placed on IR with a designation to return.

Newton’s pectoral muscle injury will land him on IR, but, like Tunsil, there’s still a chance he could be available later this season, so designating him for return on cutdown day keeps the door open for Washington.

The Commanders brought back Settle and signed Omenihu to add needed depth at the position. Newton’s injury pushes Tuttle up as the top reserve.

Cowart gets the last spot because of his experience, but like others near the bottom of the depth chart, his spot could change depending on roster needs and who becomes available.

Linebacker (4): Frankie Luvu, Sonny Styles, Leo Chenal, Jordan Magee

There are no real surprises here. Kain Medrano and Ale Kaho were possibilities for a fifth linebacker spot, but both seem likely to clear waivers, meaning Washington could sign them back to the practice squad and continue to develop them and have them ready for a few game-day call-ups.

Outside linebacker (4): Odafe Oweh, K’Lavon Chaisson, Joshua Josephs, Javontae Jean-Baptiste

*Dorance Armstrong is placed on the reserve/suspended list

The NFL suspended Armstrong for the season opener for violating the personal conduct policy, which temporarily clears a roster spot. Jean-Baptiste missed much of last season due to a pectoral injury and didn’t show much in the early going of camp. If Washington’s outside linebackers finished camp healthy and available, Jean-Baptiste may have been hard-pressed to get a spot, but Armstrong’s suspension and injuries to Oweh (calf) and Chaisson (knee) — Quinn has not provided a timetable for their return — make it worth keeping him.

Cornerback (5): Mike Sainristil, Amik Robertson, Trey Amos, Rasul Douglas, Fabian Moreau

There are a number of outstanding questions about this group, none bigger than the availability of Amos. The 2025 second-round pick was Washington’s most consistent corner last year, but a fractured fibula cut his season short and cost him the entire offseason. He returned two weeks into camp but suffered an ankle sprain in his second practice. It’s unclear if he will be available for Week 1.

Washington added Douglas and Moreau to give the team more veteran experience and depth, and both proved their worth.

Whenever Amos returns, it’ll be interesting to see whether Robertson or Sainristil shifts inside to the slot.

Safety (5): Nick Cross, Jeremy Reaves, Quan Martin, Percy Butler, Tyler Owens

Washington’s most notable roster cut happened Tuesday. Will Harris was the team’s top safety during his limited time last season (he missed eight games because of a fractured fibula), but the addition of Cross in free agency pushed him down the depth chart. Butler and Owens have been staples on special teams and became even more important when special teams ace Nick Bellore retired.

Martin struggled last season, but his two preseason interceptions made the decision to move on from Harris an obvious one.

Special teams (3)

P/H Tress Way, K Drew Stevens, LS Tyler Ott

text:
Transcript

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

Just as football season kicks back into gear, a new study was released this week about former NFL players and the degenerative brain disease known as CTE. Researchers found that at least a quarter of former NFL players who died between the years of 2016 and 2021 had CTE, which is associated with symptoms like memory loss and mood swings. So with millions of youngsters set to play youth and high school football this fall, families and officials are renewing conversations about safety. NPR's Becky Sullivan has the story.

(SOUNDBITE OF WHISTLE BLOWING)

BECKY SULLIVAN, BYLINE: It's a lovely late afternoon in Tonawanda, New York, the sun shining low over the football field at Kenney Park. More than a hundred kids are here, split up by age, practicing blocks and tackles.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Let's go, folks.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Ready.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Low. Come out strong together. Ready. Set.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Ready.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Go. Good. Drive your feet. Keep driving. Keep driving.

SULLIVAN: About 20 miles away is the NFL stadium where the Buffalo Bills play. So all the boys here are wearing full-on Bills gear - white jerseys, blue pants, helmets, pads, the works.

JONATHAN ELIAS: Yes. Bills everything. We got lights, lamps, carpets (laughter), you name it.

SULLIVAN: Jonathan Elias (ph) is a huge Bills fan. His two young sons are out on the field, Dom (ph) and Caleb (ph).

ELIAS: Forty-four to the right. Eleven's right there to the left. He's the one that can't stand still - can't sit still, dancing and moving, everything else, in line.

SULLIVAN: We asked whether he'd seen the new study that put that stark number on CTE and former NFL players. Elias hadn't, but he's always been worried about the risk of brain injury for his sons.

ELIAS: Oh, definitely - with all the concussions and everything that can happen, all the movies and articles and everything that we see.

SULLIVAN: Not every kid who plays football will get CTE - far from it. The risk of developing the disease goes up the longer a player's football career goes on. Still, though, CTE has been found in the brains of some people who only played through high school, and about 1 million American high schoolers will play 11-on-11 football this fall.

MICHAEL KRUEGER: When the article came out this week - we're aware of it, we shared it, you know, and talked about it.

SULLIVAN: This is Michael Krueger (ph). He's the director of the Colorado High School Activities Association, which oversees all high school sports in the state. This past week's news won't move the needle too much in Colorado, he says, because the needle has already been moving for years now.

KRUEGER: So in terms of change, I think it's ongoing. I don't think it's all of a sudden, we're going to go, oh, my gosh, you know, this article came out. Let's look at football. I think it's constantly being evaluated for ways we can improve the game.

SULLIVAN: He points to new recommendations issued just earlier this summer by the National Federation of State High School Associations. It advised that schools ban certain drills, like the Oklahoma drill, where two players line up in a tight area, then run right at each other, full speed, full strength, in a classic football test of toughness. Krueger says Colorado wasted no time in enacting those recommendations.

KRUEGER: Colorado was right at the forefront of that, and we started out with - you know, to remove those drills from our high school football practices. We shouldn't be doing those anymore.

SULLIVAN: Dr. Greg Canty is the director of sports medicine at Children's Mercy in Kansas City. He's been seeing patients for about 20 years now. These days, he gets a lot more questions than he used to from young athletes and their families about football and concussions.

GREG CANTY: When I first started practicing sports medicine, those conversations were ones I may have wanted to have as a physician, but no one else really interested in hearing it as much.

SULLIVAN: Canty saw the new study, of course. He points out that the cohort of former NFL players the researchers looked at had largely played their pro careers a long time ago, like in the 1970s, '80s and '90s.

CANTY: And so I don't know how to take the data that was recently released and apply that to my young athletes, other than trying to let their families know there's probably never been a safer time to play youth sports because of the recognition when it comes to concussion, because of the recognition we now have.

SULLIVAN: Football, he says, definitely does have more risk for injury than non-collision sports. But there's benefits, too, he says. Research has shown better mental health outcomes for kids who play team sports.

(SOUNDBITE OF WHISTLE BLOWING)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Hurry up. Hustle up.

SULLIVAN: Back in New York, the peewee kids are mostly just running around with the ball. Mom Nicole Brogan (ph) is watching from the sidelines, dressed in green scrubs. She's a nurse - works at a high school, where she has seen plenty of athletes come through with concussions. So she was hesitant to sign up her 6-year-old son, Cooper (ph), for tackle football, she said. But her dad told her, let him be a kid, and convinced her Cooper would learn things bigger than the game.

NICOLE BROGAN: Respect for the adults and for the teammates. Even if one kid goes down, everyone drops and takes a knee. They all will help the players up. It's very good community.

SULLIVAN: And at the end of the day, playing football makes Cooper happy.

BROGAN: Even before practice, I'm like, try to rest a little so that your body's good to go. No, he's outside throwing the football with my dad. After the games, they are out here, throwing, he's - any chance he can.

SULLIVAN: It's tough to beat making your kid that happy. So for now, she says she'll place her trust in the equipment and the coaches and hope for the best.

Becky Sullivan, NPR News.

title: Patriots roster cuts 2026: How they will get below the 53-man limit - Pats Pulpit
description:
ET, they and the other 31 teams in the NFL need to be under the league-mandated 53-man roster limit.
In order to stay on top of every move, please make sure to visit our Patriots roster cuts tracker as well as our regularly updated Patriots depth chart.
Again, we encourage you to follow our Patriots roster cuts tracker to stay on top of all the latest developments.
If they are awarded a player, they have one hour to make room for him on their active 53-man roster.
In order not to get lost amid all the action — one final time — please make sure to bookmark and regularly visit our Patriots roster cuts tracker.
text:
Preseason and training camp are in the rear-view mirror, and all that is left for the New England Patriots to do before the start of the regular season is put the finishing touches on their 53-man roster.

That process will be an ongoing one throughout the year, but Sunday will see a first major deadline. By 6 p.m. ET, they and the other 31 teams in the NFL need to be under the league-mandated 53-man roster limit. This means that more than 1,000 players will be out of a job — in some cases temporarily, in others permanently — included several previously employed by the Patriots.

In order to stay on top of every move, please make sure to visit our Patriots roster cuts tracker as well as our regularly updated Patriots depth chart. As for cutdown day itself, here is what to expect this weekend, and what all of that means for New England.

How do NFL roster cuts work?

The Patriots can reduce the number of players on their active roster in multiple ways. The most straight-forward of which is simply cutting a player to remove him from the active roster. However, as with all things pro football, there is some nuance to the process.

The league, after all, makes a distinction between players getting waived or released based on their experience.

Waived: Players with less than four years of experience (i.e. having been on an active roster or injury list for a minimum of six weeks) will be placed on the waiver wire and therefore available to any other team. Based on the 2026 draft order, clubs can put in an indefinite number of claims on players as long as roster capacities and the salary cap are not violated.

As Super Bowl runners-up, the Patriots currently hold 31st priority meaning that their chances of success project to be lower than last year, when they were fourth.

Teams have until Monday, Aug. 31 at 1 p.m. ET to submit claims and then another hour to add any pickups to their 53-man rosters. This means that spots on the active team need to either be open or created for any waiver claim to join because those claims cannot be rejected. If a player clears waivers unclaimed, he enters free agency just like vested veterans do. A player would then be free to sign with any team’s active roster or practice squad, including his original one.

Additionally, teams can waive players with an injury designation. If they go unclaimed, they would automatically revert to a team’s injured reserve list — a process the Patriots are quite familiar with, having employed it on rookie running back Myles Montgomery earlier during the summer.

Released: As opposed to the players headed for waivers, so-called vested veterans have four or more years of service under their respective belts. They will get released and hit free agency right away, meaning that they are eligible to negotiate with any team without first having to pass through the waiver wire.

How does injured reserve work?

To reduce the number of players under contract, teams can also place them on one of the reserve lists available. Among them is injured reserve (IR), which is used on players that, as the name suggests, have suffered an injury and will be out for an extended period of time. Players will need to miss at least four games when sent to IR.

Up until 2023, any player moved there before 4:01 p.m. ET on the second post-cutdown day would have been ineligible to be reactivated later during the season. The NFL, however, changed those rules in 2024.

As a result, teams can now reactivate up to two players sent to IR on the final day of roster cuts (i.e. Sunday before 6 p.m. ET). If New England, for example, moves up to two of its currently-injured players such as offensive lineman Ben Brown or linebacker Khalil Jacobs there and designates them for return, they would not count against the initial 53-man roster limit but still be permitted to come back after the first four weeks of the season. At that point, follow-up moves to create space on the 53-man team will be necessary.

Overall, clubs are allowed to bring eight players back from IR during the season. Like those moved there on the day of final cuts, they will have to sit out a minimum of four games before being allowed to return to the 53-man roster. A player cannot go through this process more than twice a year.

Players not designated to return ahead of the 4 p.m. ET deadline on Tuesday, or already sent to IR at an earlier point this year, are out for the season. In order for them to return to an active roster at a future point, they would have to be cut from IR with an injury settlement, something the Patriots did with running back Terrell Jennings and interior offensive lineman Andrew Rupcich earlier in training camp. Once the agreed-upon settlement period ends, they are eligible to sign with any team or, three weeks after that, return to their original one.

How do PUP and NFI work?

Besides sending players to injured reserve, teams can also move them to the physically unable to perform (PUP) or non-football injury/illness (NFI) lists. There is a caveat, though: they already have to be on those lists come cutdown day to actually be sent there; players typically are moved to PUP or NFI at the start of training camp but players cannot join either retroactively.

Currently, only two Patriots are on those lists:

ED Harold Landry (active/PUP)

S Brenden Schooler (active/NFI)

What is the difference between those two? In the most basic of terms, it all comes down to the origin of the injury necessitating a move to one of the lists in the first place.

If it happened at the team’s facility or during an NFL game, a player can be sent to PUP. If the injury happened in college or outside of team supervision, NFI is the place to go.

The main difference from a functional perspective, however, is player compensation. While players on PUP are entitled to their salary, those on NFI are not. Teams can still elect to pay them their contractually agreed-upon base salary, but the CBA allows them to renegotiate a different number.

If a player starts training camp on either list, their status — as seen above — will be set to “active,” which means that they count against the roster limit A team then has two options: either remove them from the list and send them to the 53-man team ahead of the roster cutdown deadline, or keep them on PUP or NFI and flip the switch to “reserve” status. At that point, they would have to sit out at least four games before being allowed to re-join the club.

A player is ineligible to be moved back to PUP or NFI once they have participated in practice or played in a game. Any longer-term follow-up injuries would require a move to injured reserve.

How else can a roster be reduced?

Besides the methods mentioned above, teams also have a handful of other tools at their disposal, all of them pretty self-explanatory.

Reserve/retired: If a player retires, he will be moved there and no longer count against the roster limit. A team retains his rights for however long he is on that list and contractually bound to the team.

Reserve/suspended or Commissioner’s exempt list: Both lists deal with players potentially facing league discipline or are in legal limbo. The first is relevant for all types of infractions as classified by the NFL, the latter can be used by commissioner Roger Goodell’s to keep players from participating in team activities if there are ongoing investigations or other matters possible impacting their status.

Trade: Not much to explain here. Teams could decide to trade players to get them off the team. Obviously, player-for-player moves or simply acquiring a player via trade in exchange for a draft pick also is an option. Neither of those scenarios would reduce the roster count, though.

What does this mean for the Patriots?

By using the methods explained above, the Patriots and the rest of the NFL will have to bring their active rosters under the 53-player limit by Sunday, 6 p.m. ET. As of Saturday morning, New England still carries a full 91 players on its team, including roster-exempt offensive tackle Lorenz Metz.

Metz, a participant in the NFL’s International Player Pathway Program, will have to be either officially make the 53-man roster or be removed via one of the methods outlined above.

Of course, any and all transactions over the coming days may be reported ahead of the 6 p.m. ET deadline on Sunday; teams also could wait significantly longer before making any moves public. Again, we encourage you to follow our Patriots roster cuts tracker to stay on top of all the latest developments.

Once roster cutdowns are over, the scramble for talent begins. As noted above, clubs have until 1 p.m. ET on Monday to put waiver claims in to acquire non-vested players. If they are awarded a player, they have one hour to make room for him on their active 53-man roster. For more on the waiver wire process, please click here.

Upon “receipt of the subsequent personnel notice,” teams can also start building their practice squads. Up to 16 players can be signed with six of those spots available for players regardless of their experience in the NFL.

A little bit further down the line lies the end of the NFL’s Top 51 rule. All contracts on the 53-man roster, plus those on practice squads and injured reserve, will then start counting against the salary cap throughout the regular season.

Have the Patriots made some moves?

As noted above, New England have not made any moves so far. They will be coming as early as Saturday, however. In order not to get lost amid all the action — one final time — please make sure to bookmark and regularly visit our Patriots roster cuts tracker.

text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — His team had just dispatched the Houston Texans in Friday’s preseason finale when Dave Canales’ thoughts quickly turned to the roster math facing the Carolina Panthers’ decision-makers this weekend.

Asked about rookie quarterback Haynes King, who had a terrific debut in the Hall of Fame Game but then missed the next three with a hamstring injury, Canales started working through the numbers at quarterback — and several other offensive positions.

“(Quarterback is) another decision. You talk about (running back) AJ Dillon, who had a great camp. Do you keep three quarterbacks? Four running backs?” Canales said. “How do you keep all these numbers — seven receivers, eight receivers that we’re talking about? The loaded tight end room of guys that we trust.

“So yeah, we got our work cut out for us in the next couple days.”

That work will start in earnest Saturday, when the Panthers’ first wave of early cuts is expected before Sunday’s 6 p.m. deadline to take rosters from 90 to 53 players.

Canales is right: This year’s roster projection was tricky business. But we’re rolling out one more version before the cuts start coming.

Changes from last week’s projection are noted in bold.

Quarterbacks (3)

On: Bryce Young, Kenny Pickett, Haynes King

Notable cut: Kyle Trask

The last time we saw King, the undrafted free agent from Georgia Tech was making plays with his arm and legs in a win over the Arizona Cardinals in the Hall of Fame Game. Then he strained his hamstring diving into the end zone and aggravated it in the celebration that ensued. That left only August game tape for other teams to dig into — plus another 46 over King’s six college seasons. King said he believes he could have played Friday, but the team held him so the injury doesn’t nag him all season. He said the Panthers have given him no indication whether he’ll stick around. Asked if he thinks he could be claimed by another team, King said: “I’m not really looking into that. I love it here. … It feels like home.” One option: Teams can put up to two players on injured reserve before cuts and designate them to return, but they must sit out at least four games.

Running backs (4)

On: Chuba Hubbard, Jonathon Brooks, Trevor Etienne, AJ Dillon

Notable cut: N/A

After Hubbard returned too quickly from a calf injury last season, the team has taken a cautious approach with his hamstring strain so he can be 100 percent for Week 1. Brooks has looked strong in his return from a second ACL surgery, and his catch in a scramble situation was one of the few highlights for the first-team offense in the joint practice Wednesday with Houston. Etienne left Friday’s game after the first series with an ankle injury that will require imaging. Dillon had nine touches against the Texans, but averaged only 2 yards a carry.

Tight ends (4)

On: Tommy Tremble, Ja’Tavion Sanders, Mitchell Evans, Feleipe Franks

Notable cut: Darren Waller

The Panthers signed Waller to a one-year deal for the veteran minimum of $1.3 million because they wanted to add competition to the tight end room. They also gave themselves options. If Waller is on the active roster for the first regular-season game, his deal becomes fully guaranteed. So they could choose to keep him on the practice squad initially, though they’d risk losing him to any interested team. General manager Dan Morgan could try to move Sanders, who’s been the subject of trade rumors.

Asked about Waller’s roster prospects, Canales said: “It’s certainly Dan and I looking at how we’re gonna use him and how he fits into the whole picture. And then of course it’s Darren, it’s his representation, making sure this is the right situation. And right now they feel like it is. But again those conversations have to happen and we’ll be making that decision in the next couple days.”

Receivers (6)

On: Tetairoa McMillan, Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette, Brycen Tremayne, Jimmy Horn, Ja’seem Reed

Injured reserve: Chris Brazzell, Dan Chisena

Notable cuts: David Moore, John Metchie, Casey Washington

Canales pointed to the receiver room as one of the strongest competitions. Horn played his way onto the roster with a strong finish in camp, including an eye-opening performance at Jacksonville when he made impact plays in the pass, run and return games. Moore has long been a favorite of Canales, but it feels like the final spot will come down to Metchie and Reed, who caught two passes for 37 yards Friday after missing the Jags game with a calf injury. Reed is younger and taller than Metchie, and can play more WR spots. Metchie has return ability. Tough call.

Offensive line (9)

On: Rasheed Walker, Monroe Freeling, Robert Hunt, Damien Lewis, Luke Fortner, Sam Hecht, Brady Christensen, Stone Forsythe, Albert Reese

NFI/PUP lists: Taylor Moton, Ikem Ekwonu

Notable cut: Chandler Zavala, Jake Curhan

Freeling had a day to forget in the joint practice against the Texans, allowing at least four of the seven sacks Houston had on Young. The first-round pick from Georgia was overmatched against Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson. But with Moton and Ekwonu out indefinitely, the Panthers will take their lumps with Freeling as he tries to expedite his learning curve. I don’t have a great sense of what Morgan will do with the last OL spot or two. Reese was one of Pro Football Focus’ highest-rated rookies entering play Friday, but allowed a sack and four pressures against the Texans. But 6-foot-7, 325-pound dudes don’t grow on trees.

Defensive line (5)

On: Derrick Brown, Bobby Brown, Lee Hunter, Cam Jackson, Jared Harrison-Hunte

PUP list: Tershawn Wharton

Notable cut: Aaron Hall

Canales wants to get both Derrick Brown and Bobby Brown a little more work during what amounts to a bye week after both missed time in camp with injuries. That gave young players like Hunter, the second-round pick from Texas Tech, Harrison-Hunte and Hall opportunities to show what they could do. This group still feels a little thin depth-wise, so don’t be surprised if Morgan tries to add to it. But it helps to have a Pro Bowler anchoring things. “It starts with the trenches,” Derrick Brown said this week. “Whoever wins the line of scrimmage wins the game. We know that.”

Outside linebackers (5)

On: Jaelan Phillips, Patrick Jones, Princely Umanmielen, Trevis Gipson, Thomas Incoom

Notable cuts: Cam Gill, Jeremiah Moon

IR: Nic Scourton

I had Gipson as one of the last cuts last week. But the 6-4, 264-pound Gipson made more plays than Gill as camp came to a close. The 29-year-old was active early against the Texans, sacking Davis Mills on Houston’s first offensive possession and then pressuring him on Lathan Ransom’s interception the next series. Incoom had a tackle for loss Friday, but his real value is as a four-phase special teams player.

Linebackers (5)

On: Devin Lloyd, Trevin Wallace, Claudin Cherelus, Bam Martin-Scott, Jackson Kuwatch

Notable cut: Maema Njongmeta

International Player Program exemption: Maz Mwansa

The competition between Wallace and Cherelus for the second starting spot has received a lot of attention this summer, arguably more than it deserves. Why? Because the Panthers are in nickel a lot under Ejiro Evero, who likes using three-safety looks with Lloyd the lone inside linebacker. Wallace’s first-quarter sack of Mills was an example of the blitzing ability that could separate him from Cherelus.

Cornerbacks (5)

On: Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, Chau Smith-Wade, Will Lee, Akayleb Evans

Notable cuts: Corey Thornton, Devonta Smith, Robert Rochell

Special teams will be the determining factor for the last couple of spots on the 53. And the Panthers view Evans as their best gunner. So we’re giving him the edge over Thornton, who has struggled in coverage throughout the preseason. Smith, the undrafted free agent from Notre Dame, had two pass breakups and a run stop in one defensive series in the first half. He probably won’t make the 53, but the Panthers would love to sneak him through waivers and sign him back to the practice squad.

Safeties (4)

On: Tre’von Moehrig, Nick Scott, Lathan Ransom, Zakee Wheatley

Notable cuts: Isaiah Simmons, Demani Richardson

The Panthers have improved their safety depth with a pair of Day-3 draft picks in Ransom and Wheatley, both of whom have had strong preseasons. Wheatley, the rookie from Penn State, proved to be a willing tackler, while Ransom has never shied away from a bone-jarring tackle — practice included. Ransom had a first-half interception Friday.

Specialists (3)

On: Sam Martin (punter), Ryan Fitzgerald (kicker), J.J. Jansen (long snapper)

Notable cuts: N/A

Same as it ever was, especially the seemingly ageless long snapper.

title: Marvin Mims Jr. Exits Broncos' Preseason Finale With New Injury - Sports Illustrated
description:
Marvin Mims Jr. made his preseason debut on Friday night against the Minnesota Vikings.
After missing the Denver Broncos' first two games with a soft-tissue injury suffered a week into training camp, the team decided to give Mims some exhibition action in the preseason finale.
The Broncos may rue that decision after he suffered a foot injury at the end of the first drive of the night.
Mims is questionable to return with a foot injury.
Update After the game, head coach Sean Payton addressed the Mims injury.
text:
Marvin Mims Jr. made his preseason debut on Friday night against the Minnesota Vikings.

After missing the Denver Broncos' first two games with a soft-tissue injury suffered a week into training camp, the team decided to give Mims some exhibition action in the preseason finale. The Broncos may rue that decision after he suffered a foot injury at the end of the first drive of the night.

Mims got up gingerly, and limped to the sideline, where he threw his helmet down in frustration. Trainers escorted him to the blue tent on the sideline, and shortly after, the fourth-year returner headed for the locker room.

Mims is questionable to return with a foot injury.

Even if it's not a serious injury, there's absolutely no reason to send Mims back out there against the Vikings. It was a mistake to even play him, to be honest.

On one hand, I understand the impulse to get Mims some live-bullet reps. On the other hand, the Broncos are well acquainted with his ability. Did they really need to see him in an exhibition setting?

It was an unnecessary risk. We can only hope it's nothing serious.

A Distinguished Bronco

Mims was the Broncos' second-round draft pick in 2023. The first draft pick of the Sean Payton era quickly distinguished himself, earning Pro Bowl and All-Pro honors as a returner in both of his first two seasons. Mims joined Von Miller as the only players in Broncos history to achieve that feat in his first two seasons.

As stalwart as Mims has been on special teams, he's yet to find that kind of success on offense as a pro. However, when the Broncos have utilized him, he's always come up big.

Mims has the clutch gene, making big plays when it matters most in critical situations. In the playoffs last year, the Broncos dealt with injuries to wide receivers Troy Franklin and Pat Bryant, which pushed Mims and Lil'Jordan Humphrey onto the field.

Both answered the bell, but especially Mims, who scored a clutch-time touchdown in the Broncos' 33-30 overtime win over the Buffalo Bills in the divisional round and made some big plays the following week against the New England Patriots in the AFC championship game. When it was all said and done, Denver's playoff run ended early thanks to Bo Nix's untimely injury, but Mims finished as the team's leading receiver in the postseason.

It was a great way to punctuate Mims's third NFL season. Entering a contract year, there's been much speculation and debate on whether the Broncos will extend him.

There's been no extension yet. It didn't help that Mims got hurt a week into training camp, and if this foot ends up costing him any time, it can only further delay a possible new deal.

The Takeaway

Hopefully, the injury is minor. If it isn't, the good news is that Denver has found some great returner talent in the undrafted ranks this summer.

Kolbe Katsis, Cameron Ross, and Sean Fresch Jr. are players to watch, depending again on Mims's health outlook.

We'll keep a close eye on the Mims situation and provide an update as soon as we know anything.

Update

After the game, head coach Sean Payton addressed the Mims injury.

“Mims is going to be fine," Payton said. "It’s a bruise.”

text:
Following the 49ers’ final preseason game on Thursday night in Las Vegas, the real work began for coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch.

The 49ers have an abundance of injury questions entering Week 1, but only wide receiver Ricky Pearsall was lost for the 2026 NFL season this summer.

All NFL teams must reduce their rosters from 90 players to the 53-man limit by Sunday at 3 p.m.

And the medical reports will determine how the 49ers piece it together ahead of their trip to Melbourne, Australia, to face the Los Angeles Rams on Thursday, Sept. 10.

“That's why you want as long as possible,” Shanahan said. “They're moving it up this year on Sunday with us leaving for Australia so soon. So it just makes it a little bit harder to guess where those guys are going to be.

“Most of our guys, besides Ricky, are going to be all right. How good are they going to be Week 1? How good are they going to be Week 2? Those are things we've got to balance out.”

And that is why projecting the 49ers’ initial 53-man roster becomes so difficult.

Teams are allowed to designate two players to return off injured reserve on Sunday. All other players who are ticketed for injured reserve must first be included on the 53-man roster.

Here is our final 49ers roster projection:

Quarterback (3)

Brock Purdy

Mac Jones

Kurtis Rourke

Also: Adrian Martinez

Although Rourke sustained broken ribs in his only game of the preseason, he has shown enough to make the 49ers believe he could be the backup quarterback next season. If the 49ers keep two QBs on their opening roster, they run the risk of losing him.

Running back (4)

Christian McCaffrey

Kyle Juszczyk

Kaelon Black

Jordan James

PUP - Isaac Guerendo

Also, Khalil Herbert, Sincere McCormick

This is a position where the 49ers can go a little light from the outset. As a vested veteran, the 49ers can re-sign Herbert on Monday after spots on the roster open with additional players being placed on injured reserve. Herbert has value as a reserve after appearing in 63 games (13 starts) over the past five seasons.

Mike Evans

De’Zhaun Stribling

Deebo Samuel

Demarcus Robinson

Jordan Watkins

Jacob Cowing

IR - Christian Kirk

Also, Malik Turner, KhaDarel Hodge, Trenton Irwin, Will Pauling, Wesley Grimes

The 49ers have good depth at this position, and it looks as if the top six are set with Cowing getting the nod because of his history of returning punts. The other players who have been fielding punts do not have much experience in college or the pros.

Tight end (3)

George Kittle

Jake Tonges

Luke Farrell

Also, Brayden Willis, Hayden Rucci, Khalil Dinkins

It remains to be seen if Kittle will travel with his teammates to Australia for the Week 1 game. If he remains back in the Bay Area for more physical therapy, strength and conditioning training, the 49ers could elevate a tight end from the practice squad, such as Willis or Rucci, to be available to play against the Rams.

Shanahan has yet to announce whom the team will start at left guard for Week 1, but it’s looking as if Willis, a rookie, could get that call. Pleasants (knee) and Jones (calf) are expected back soon from injuries, so it appears they might avoid stints on IR. Cruz showed enough as the summer went on to believe that he could develop as a starter down the road.

Also, Ogba Okoronkwo, Sebastian Valdez, Evan Anderson, Quinton Bell, Viliami Fehoko Jr., Jah Joyner

Okoronkwo, a seven-year veteran, had a good camp, and the 49ers certainly can keep him around on the practice squad as insurance. Valdez made a good run at a roster spot, so he still has a chance to contribute at some point in the season, too. It was a tough call between Eason and Thompson Jr., so they both get spots on the team.

Linebacker (5)

Fred Warner

Dre Greenlaw

Jaden Dugger

Tatum Bethune

Garret Wallow

IR - Nick Martin, Luke Gifford

Also, Deion Jones, Jalen Graham, Larry Worth III

Martin earned a spot on the team, but his hamstring injury in the second preseason game likely means that he will be forced to open the season on the injured list. Gifford also is trying to get back from a hamstring injury he sustained early in training camp.

Renardo Green

Upton Stout

Jack Jones

Darrell Luter

Ephesians Prysock

IR - Nate Hobbs

Also, Jakob Robinson, Eli Apple

Green sustained a hamstring injury in the second preseason game, so it is possible Jones could open as the starter with Luter slated to be the top backup. Prysock sustained a shoulder injury that could limit him early in the season, but he is likely ticketed to a developmental role as a rookie, anyway.

Safety (4)

Ji’Ayir Brown

Marques Sigle

Siran Neal

Ashtyn Davis

IR - Malik Mustapha

Also, Jalen Stroman, Patrick McMorris

The 49ers could create a roster spot at the cut to 53 players by releasing Neal or Davis, or both. Because they are vested veterans, they would not be subject to the waiver wire, so the 49ers simply could re-sign them the following day when they place other players on injured reserve. The wild card is Mustapha. There is no clear indication at this point whether his hamstring injury will force him to open the season on injured reserve.

Special teams (3)

K Eddy Piñeiro

P Corliss Waitman

LS Jon Weeks

The 49ers are in a much better position with their specialists than a year ago. Remember, they broke camp last year with Jake Moody as their kicker. Piñeiro is coming off a final exhibition game in which he kicked six field goals, including makes from 48, 59, 51 and 54 yards. It appears the 49ers are vastly improved at punter, too, with Waitman taking Thomas Morstead’s place.

For the past three seasons, Zach Charbonnet and Kenneth Walker III were arguably the NFL’s top rushing tag team. Both backs would routinely get double-digt carries per game in the Seattle backfield.

Things will look much different for the Seahawks’ rushing attack this season, however, particularly early in the year. Walker III is now in Kansas City after signing as a free agent, and Charbonnet is injured after tearing his ACL last season.

Below, we will deliver a Charbonnet injury update, and look at when he is expected to return.

Zach Charbonnet injury update: When will Seahawks RB be back?Charbonnet tore his ACL in the Seahawks’ Divisional Round win over the 49ers this past January. It was assumed at the time that this injury would put the running back on the shelf for the early portion of the 2026-27 season, and that is the case.

The Seahawks placed Charbonnet on the physically unable to perform list prior to the start of training camp.

Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald weighed in on Charbonnet’s rehab progress earlier this month.

“It’s just a progression that you’ve got to be able to do to get your body ready to play, especially at the running back position,” Macdonald said in a video recorded by hawkblogger.com’s Brian Nemhauser. “He’s going through it, hitting his hurdles, and we’re rolling … We’ll see what the timetable is and how quickly he comes back.”

It typically takes 9-12 months for NFL players to return from ACL tears.

One current example of an NFL player bouncing back relatively quickly from an ACL tear is Packers tight end Tucker Kraft.

Kraft tore his ACL on November 2 of last year. Ten months later, he is in line to start Week 1 of the regular season.

Nine months from Charbonnet’s injury would be October 17, 2026. Ten months from Charbonnet’s injury would be November 17, 2026.

The earliest we could likely see Charbonnet back on the field for the Seahawks is Week 7 against the Chiefs. More likely is that Seattle waits until after its bye week, which takes place in Week 11, to bring Charbonnet back into the fold.

Here is a look at the Seahawks’ schedule around the time that Charbonnet is expected to be back.

Week 9 Sunday, November 8: Cardinals at Seahawks

Week 10 Sunday, November 15: Seahawks at Raiders

Week 11 Sunday, November 22: Bye week

Week 12 Sunday, November 29: Seahawks at 49ers

Week 13 Monday, December 7: Cowboys at Seahawks

Zach Charbonnet fantasy football ADP and odds

Charbonnet has a fantasy football ADP of 124 at FantasyPros.

One popular fantasy strategy that is often employed by owners this time of year is to stash quality players that have longterm injuries, like Charbonnet, on their bench. Many will pick a kicker in the final round of their draft, drop the kicker, add an injured player like Charbonnet, place him on IR, and then re-add a kicker.

Charbonnet is currently +5000 at Fanatics Sportsbook to win NFL Comeback Player of the Year honors. He is one of the longshots, for sure, as the likes of Patrick Mahomes (+190) and Kyler Murray (+450) sit atop the board.

Charbonnet, who is 25-years-old, put up career numbers last season as he rushed for 730 yards and had 12 rushing touchdowns. He also caught 24 balls for 144 yards.

Seahawks odds

The defending champions are, to no one’s surprise, one of the favorites to win this season’s Super Bowl. Macdonald’s crew is currently +1100 at Fanatics to win it all. Only the Bills and Rams have shorter odds.

The Seahawks are +215 to win the highly competitive NFC West. The Rams are the favorite at -115.

text:
The Dallas Cowboys have had good fortune this offseason when it comes to injuries and they appear to have left their preseason finale against the New Orleans Saints mostly unscathed.

There was one injury to talk about, however, as linebacker Marist Liufau exited the contest early due to a forearm injury suffered in the first half of the contest.

After the game was over, Liufau had his arm in a sling, which was the first sign he had suffered something at least somewhat significant.

Not long after that, head coach Brian Schottenheimer said that Liufau will be on the shelf for "weeks" due to a fractured forearm that will require surgery.

"Fractured his forearm, so I think he's going to have surgery as early as Monday," Schottenheimer told reporters. "What a great competitor and he'll be back."

Schottenheimer wouldn't rule out the Cowboys placing Liufau on injured reserve to begin the season.

"Yeah, we'll look at it," he said of a possible IR placement for Liufau. "Sounds like it's going to be surgical, so you're talking about some weeks, but I don't want to put a timeframe on it right now.

Because of a shift in the rules, the Cowboys will be able to place two players on injured reserve with a designation to return without having to first save them a spot on the initial 53-man roster. This might actually help Liufau stick in Dallas, as he was a clear cut candidate otherwise.

Returning players

Among the players who suffered an injury in the last preseason game or didn't suit up at all in that contest, rookie tight end Michael Trigg and safety Julius Wood returned to action.

Trigg had been battling a toe injury since suffering it in the first preseason game, but he was able to return to practice this week, which was a clear indication he would play in preseason Week 3.

Trigg, who is trying to grab the TE3 spot or force the Cowboys to carry a fourth tight end, did not record a catch on three targets. He'll likely be kept on the practice squad if he's cut and passes through waivers.

Wood, who came back from a concussion, has been a standout throughout the offseason and gave Markquese Bell a run for his money for the final safety spot. Both players saw snaps Friday, with Wood finishing with six tackles and Bell posting two.

As good as Wood played, Schottenheimer's effusive praise of Bell's special teams prowess during the week is a strong hint he's going to make the cut, which leaves Wood in a precarious spot.

Who's still hurt?

Defensive lineman Jonathan Bullard, who has missed extensive time this offseason due to injury, was sidelined once again. He failed to play in a single preseason game and his status for the regular season opener remains up in the air.

Rookie tight end DJ Rogers was another injured player who didn't suit up. Rogers got hurt in practice last week and hasn't been seen since. He's going to miss the cut, but is a candidate for the practice squad if healthy.
